entry.title: Discovery Fills a Gap in Understanding Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia

media:group.media:title: Discovery Fills a Gap in Understanding Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia
media:group.media:description:
Scientists recently revealed mutations in two additional genes that disrupt the ability of motile cilia to perform functions such as clearing mucus from the airways, causing disease.
A team led by researchers at Harvard Medical School and University Children’s Hospital Münster in Germany unveiled the detailed structure and composition of an understudied part of the cilium known as the transition zone — revealing that abnormalities in this zone can play a role in the rare disease primary ciliary dyskinesia.
In addition to improving understanding of cilia biology, the research could help explain some of the 20% to 30% of PCD cases that have no known genetic cause and find new ways to treat this disease.

entry.title: Medical Simulation "Escape Room" Prepares Students for Clinical Rotations

media:group.media:title: Medical Simulation "Escape Room" Prepares Students for Clinical Rotations
media:group.media:description:
Second-year medical and dental students are gearing up for their clinical rotations by competing in a medical simulation "escape room."
Students from each academic society competed in groups to perform procedures, make diagnoses, and solve medical-related puzzles in the shortest amount of time. This was the first time the students weren’t completely guided by a faculty member during their hands-on clinical skills.
“I think a lot of times students struggle when they’re transitioning from the preclinical years because you have so much knowledge and you just don’t always know how to apply it,” said Suellen Li, HMS instructor of medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. “It’s a matter of sorting through what’s relevant, what knowledge you bring to the table that is needed for the patient, and determining and triaging what you want to do next.”
The simulation is part of BRIDGES, a pre-clerkship clinical skills course in the Pathways curriculum, and was organized by HMS faculty members Jacob Koshy, Suellen Li, Victoria Mason, Patrick Smithedajkul, and Kirsten Engel.
In January, the second-year medical students will begin their Principal Clinical Experience (PCE).

entry.title: Meet David Hirsh, Co-Director of the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology

media:group.media:title: Meet David Hirsh, Co-Director of the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology
media:group.media:description:
Meet David Hirsh, who began his role as co-director of the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology (HST) this summer.
"I think the most important reason I’ve dedicated myself to transforming medical education is because our future patients, [and] the future of science, require that we inexorably find the best way to bring the next generation into their future,” Hirsh said. “It would be impossible to imagine that the methods of before will be the methods of the future.”
Hirsh, who is also an HMS professor of medicine at Cambridge Health Alliance, has made significant and far-reaching contributions to the field of medical education.
He is the advisory dean and director of the London Society, one of five HMS academic advising communities to which all HST MD students are assigned.

entry.title: Meet Harvard Medical School Dean for Students Jenny Potter

media:group.media:title: Meet Harvard Medical School Dean for Students Jenny Potter
media:group.media:description:
Meet Jenny Potter, who became the HMS dean for students in the Program in Medical Education this summer. She is excited about supporting medical and dental students throughout their journey of becoming the clinicians and scientists they hope to be.
“My favorite part about working with students is getting to know them as people and getting to know what motivates them, and also what stands in their way, and then working together to figure out ways to help them achieve their goals,” Potter said.
Potter, who is also a primary care physician and HMS professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, previously served as advisory dean and director of the Castle Society, one of five academic advising communities to which all medical and dental students are assigned, and director of student well-being programs.

entry.title: Improving Mental Health Care Through Understanding A Person's Lived Experience

media:group.media:title: Improving Mental Health Care Through Understanding A Person's Lived Experience
media:group.media:description:
Understanding a person’s lived experience with mental health problems can improve their care by making it more person-centered and personalized.
"The way a person conceptualizes their lived experience is often described as an illness narrative,” says Vikram Patel, the Paul Farmer Professor and chair of the Department of Global Health and Social Medicine. “This is essentially the story that a person tells themselves to make sense of their mental health experience, and that story often influences how they understand what causes this mental health experience, and therefore what should be done to help resolve it.”
Patel says clinicians should listen to their patients to target their needs and priorities to make care person-centered instead of diagnosis-centered.

entry.title: Academic Societies at Harvard Medical School Help Students Thrive

media:group.media:title: Academic Societies at Harvard Medical School Help Students Thrive
media:group.media:description:
Medical and dental students are placed into one of five communities to help them thrive and take full advantage of the opportunities available at Harvard Medical School and Harvard School of Dental Medicine.
The academic societies provide a community-based approach to medical education and support Harvard Medical School’s 230-year tradition of enhancing interactions between students and faculty. The Cannon, Castle, Hinton, and Peabody societies are home to Pathways MD and DMD students. Health Sciences and Technology students belong to the London society.
Students in each society are supported by an advisory dean and a small group of society advisors, who are all physicians and dentists, as well as student affairs staff.
Beyond creating a collaborative learning environment, the societies help students form lasting relationships as they navigate the dynamic and demanding path to becoming a physician or dentist.

entry.title: Cellular View of the Ovary Helps Advance Understanding of Fertility and Reproductive Health

media:group.media:title: Cellular View of the Ovary Helps Advance Understanding of Fertility and Reproductive Health
media:group.media:description:
A hidden world of cellular teamwork is taking place inside the ovary every day.
In this video, you're seeing a close-up look at that process. Researchers in the lab of David Pepin, HMS associate professor at Massachusetts General Hospital, are studying how ovarian follicles, tiny structures that contain immature egg cells, grow and develop.
The bright pink cells are egg cells, while the green cells surrounding them are called granulosa cells, which help nourish and support the egg as it grows. Using a specially engineered mouse model, researchers can make these support cells glow green, allowing them to watch how the cells interact in real time.
By seeing these cells in action, scientists can better understand how healthy follicles develop and what may happen when that process is disrupted, helping advance our understanding of fertility and reproductive health.
This video footage was provided by Alana Mermin-Bunnell, a PhD student in the Harvard-MIT Health Sciences and Technology program.

entry.title: Using MINFLUX Nanoscopy to Track How Individual Proteins Interact With Lipid Droplets

media:group.media:title: Using MINFLUX Nanoscopy to Track How Individual Proteins Interact With Lipid Droplets
media:group.media:description:
Fat isn't just stored under skin and between organs — it is temporarily stashed in almost every cell in our bodies.
Specialized proteins build, modify, and break down this fat, which is stored in tiny cellular compartments called lipid droplets. When key proteins fail to reach these droplets, it can contribute to metabolic disorders like fatty liver disease and obesity and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.
Postdoctoral fellow Arda Mizrak works in the lab of Professor Wade Harper, chair of the Department of Cell Biology, examining how these proteins move within the cell.
Using MINFLUX nanoscopy at the HMS Neurobiology Imaging Facility, the researchers tracked the paths of individual proteins and directly observed how they interact with the surface of lipid droplets — something that had never been done at this scale.
Mizrak and his team found that proteins don't find lipid droplets by accident — they get briefly trapped by tiny lipid-rich regions on the droplets' surface.
By identifying the way the proteins travel, the work opens new opportunities to understand how metabolism becomes disrupted in disease, and ultimately to find new ways to make cells healthy again.

entry.title: Utsa's Day in the Life as a Harvard Medical School Postdoctoral Fellow at Boston Children's Hospital

media:group.media:title: Utsa's Day in the Life as a Harvard Medical School Postdoctoral Fellow at Boston Children's Hospital
media:group.media:description:
Meet Utsa Bhaduri, a Harvard Medical School research fellow at Boston Children’s Hospital working with the Precision Vaccines Program. 🔬
He conducts basic and translational research to advance precision vaccines to better protect vulnerable populations such as infants, older adults, and immunocompromised populations.
Beyond his postdoctoral research, he serves as a co-chair of the Harvard Medical Postdoc Association and a public policy fellow with the American Association of Immunologists. He recently completed the Mini-MBA program with the Harvard Griffin Graduate School or Arts and Sciences Business Club.
Bhaduri is not only pursuing discovery science, but he is also learning how science reaches people through entrepreneurship, business, and public policy, which will prepare him to lead his own lab and make a meaningful impact.

entry.title: Harvard Medical School 2026 State of the School Address

media:group.media:title: Harvard Medical School 2026 State of the School Address
media:group.media:description:
Harvard Medical School Dean George Q. Daley gave the annual State of the School address on Sept. 16, 2026.
In the face of numerous external pressures, HMS is maintaining its focus on research, education, and clinical care for the benefit of humanity, he said.
Daley laid out the institution’s response to recent challenges from the federal government and described a path forward that increases HMS’ partnerships with industry, emphasizes leadership in the development and responsible application of AI tools, and leans into the existing strengths of the School’s vast research and clinical community.
“Even as we face an unpredictable and parlous future, we remain steadfast in our collective pursuit of excellence, and we remain poised to tackle whatever that future brings,” Daley said.

entry.title: Devon's First Week at Harvard Medical School

media:group.media:title: Devon's First Week at Harvard Medical School
media:group.media:description:
After earning his PhD from Harvard, first-year student Devon Van Cura is embarking on his journey to earn his MD and become a physician-scientist.
The first week at Harvard Medical School is stacked with activities and events like the White Coat Ceremony, Introduction to the Profession, the first patient clinic, and social mixers.
Van Cura is on the MD track in the Health Sciences and Technology Program, an inter-institutional collaboration between Harvard University, Harvard Medical School, and MIT. HST is one of the world’s oldest interdisciplinary educational programs focused on translational medical science and engineering.
He decided to pursue medical training so he could bring his science closer to patients.

media:group.media:title: Welcome Harvard Medical School and Harvard School of Dental Medicine Class of 2030!
media:group.media:description:
Today we welcomed the Harvard Medical School and Harvard School of Dental Medicine Class of 2030! 🥼 🎉
Typically held during the first week of school, the White Coat Ceremony is a symbolic rite of passage at the start of their medical careers where students receive their white coats.
The future physicians and dentists celebrated the hard work it took to get to this point with friends and family.
